newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rejects Swiss comments on Nazi assets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rejects Swiss comments on Nazi assets.

text.p: The United States on Friday dismissed as "ludicrous" a Swiss official's charge that foreign critics were blackmailing Switzerland over the issue of compensation for Jews who might be entitled to money left in Swiss banks after World War Two.
"We have seen some statements by the government of Switzerland recently on this issue that were quite surprising, frankly, to see," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"We certainly reject any charges that the United States or any branch of the United States government has anything other than the best intentions on this issue," he said.

"Frankly, to make a charge that somehow an agency of the United States government is attempting to destabilise the Swiss banking system, or is blackmailing the Swiss government, is ludicrous. We saw such a charge from a very senior official of the Swiss government over the weekend."
Burns said he referred to Switzerland's economics minister, Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who made the comments just before ending a one-year rotating term as his country's president.

Delamuraz said late on Thursday he was sorry if he had offended families of Holocaust victims but repeated his view that it was not the right time to set up a compensation fund for Jews who might be entitled to money left in Swiss banks by the Nazis after World War Two.

The World Jewish Congress has proposed Switzerland set up a $250 million fund to compensate Holocaust survivors and heirs, who say Swiss banks have denied them money left there beyond the Nazis' reach.
Delamuraz stirred angry protest from the WJC on Tuesday by describing as "blackmail" demands for quick compensation for Holocaust survivors and heirs.
In a newspaper interview Delamuraz also accused foreign critics of attacking Switzerland's role as a financial centre with accusations the Swiss profited cynically from the war.
Delamuraz's reference to blackmail, made while he was still president of Switzerland, had been sharply criticised by the WJC and Israel's foreign ministry.
The State Department currently is researching its records to determine what the United States' role on Nazi assets may have been. Burns said a report would take a few months to complete.

"We feel that we have an obligation to the historical truth here. We have tens of thousands of survivors of the Holocaust who are affected by whether or not all of us as governments are doing the right thing by them," Burns said.

"And we need to look into this question of the financial assets that were stolen from Jews and others by the Nazis. We care deeply about this issue, and we're going to get to the bottom of the issue. And if the evidence from our historians leads us to even unpleasant truths about the actions of the United States government in the late 1940s, so be it."
Burns added: "People have a right to see the truth, and I think the Swiss government ought to take the same position on this issue."
